title: Jim Cramer Wants SpaceX Stock but Refuses to Buy Before Share Unlocks
excerpt: Strong AI-driven earnings tempt the Mad Money host, but a $35 billion-plus spending plan and lockup expirations through mid-2027 keep him on the sidelines.
body:
• CNBC's Jim Cramer says he wants SpaceX shares for his charitable trust but will not buy yet, despite third-quarter sales of $14.6 billion, up 161% year on year.
  • His biggest concern is supply: only about a third of SpaceX shares are freely tradable, and staggered lockup expirations run through mid-2027.
  • SpaceX guided fourth-quarter capital spending to $35 billion–$40 billion, nearly double Wall Street's $20.1 billion estimate, alongside a roughly $40 billion Apollo financing commitment for Nvidia chips.
  • The stock closed at $134.27 on November 6, down 16% from its post-earnings rally to $159.31 and 16.6% below its June 12 debut close.

Jim Cramer wants to own SpaceX. He is not willing to buy it yet. On the November 6 edition of Mad Money, the CNBC host said the company's third-quarter earnings had sharpened his interest in adding the stock to his Investing Club charitable trust, but that growth alone had not settled his concerns, TheStreet reported.

Numbers That Explain the Temptation

SpaceX reported third-quarter sales of $14.6 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, with adjusted EBITDA up 306% to $8.8 billion and diluted earnings of $0.35 a share. The growth engine is no longer rockets alone. The company's Super Intelligence division, which rents out AI computing power, generated $7.56 billion in sales and $4.95 billion in adjusted EBITDA — 52% of total sales. Cramer has said Google pays around $920 million a month for access to that computing capacity, while Anthropic's contracted monthly commitment is expected to reach $3.1 billion by December. Starlink, meanwhile, had 13.6 million consumer subscribers at the end of September, with connectivity revenue up 69%. In October, Cramer said SpaceX "could end up being Nvidia's largest client at this pace."

"I think that supply short-term could overwhelm demand."

— Jim Cramer, on SpaceX's staggered share lockup expirations

Why He Is Waiting

The first obstacle is spending. SpaceX expects fourth-quarter capital expenditures of $35 billion to $40 billion, nearly double Wall Street's $20.1 billion estimate, because AI data centres require heavy upfront investment before returns arrive. "The company's projected costs are astronomical," Cramer warned. The company also announced a roughly $40 billion financing commitment on October 26, under which an Apollo-managed entity would buy Nvidia chips and lease them to SpaceX. Cramer worries further financing could raise borrowing costs or lead to new share issuance that dilutes existing investors, though TheStreet noted SpaceX's debt-to-equity ratio stands at 0.22, below the aerospace and defence industry median of 0.315 reported by GuruFocus. A second uncertainty is corporate: SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to explore a possible combination, TechCrunch has reported, and no deal has been reached.

The Lockup Problem

Neither issue is Cramer's largest. He estimates only about one-third of SpaceX shares are freely tradable today. Staggered lockup expirations through mid-2027 could let more holders sell, increasing supply even if the business keeps growing, and he expects a better entry price to follow. The recent price action shows the risk he is pricing in: the stock rose nearly 8% to $159.31 the day after the October 20 earnings report, then retreated to $134.27 by November 6. Cramer has made the same risk-adjusted argument before — in October he noted the stock traded at roughly 137 times the next twelve months' earnings estimates, according to FactSet, while saying he already benefits from SpaceX's chip buying through the Nvidia shares his trust owns.

What Would Change His Mind

The tests ahead are execution and absorption. SpaceX operated 1.7 gigawatts of computing capacity in September; Elon Musk wants 3 gigawatts by year-end and 13 gigawatts by the end of 2027, targets that will be judged against construction progress, borrowing costs and cash returns. Starlink must keep growing beyond 13.6 million subscribers, and any Tesla combination would need clear terms for existing shareholders. Above all, the market must absorb newly tradable shares without another sharp decline. If it does, Cramer's wait could cost him gains. If selling accelerates, he gets the entry price he is holding out for.
